CITATION
:
Landman v. Daviau, 2012 ONSC 547

COURT
FILE NO.:

FS-11-17425

DATE:
January 23, 2012

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

APPLICANT

Uri Landman Husid

RESPONDENT

Hélène Marie Thérèse Daviau

Jeffery
Wilson, for the applicant father

Phyllis Brodkin and Serena Lein,
for the respondent mother

HEARD:
November 7-10 and 15-17, 2011

Perkins J.

Issues in the case

[
1
]

This case is about which court – this court or a
court in Lima, Perú – should
deal with the custody and access rights of the parents of a 5 year old girl
named Shelli.  Though a family law case involving a young child, this is
not

a custody case, and it is not to be decided on the basis of the child’s best
interests, but rather on the basis of the principles established by the Hague
Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction

[
2
]

Shelli was born in Perú to a Peruvian father and
a Canadian mother.  She was habitually and actually resident in Perú until the
mother brought her to Ontario 16
months ago.  The mother and father were and still are involved in several court
cases in Perú concerning custody of and access to Shelli, among other issues.
Under a Peruvian court order, the mother was permitted to travel to Canada with Shelli in September, 2010 to
visit her parents.  The order required her to return with Shelli to Perú in
November, 2010.  Once she got to Canada, the mother refused to return.  The father launched an application
under the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of
International Child Abduction, seeking an order for the return of Shelli to Perú.
That is the application that is before me for adjudication.  The convention has
been incorporated into our domestic law in
section 46
of the
Children’s Law
Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12.

[
3
]

The mother has invoked article 13 (b) of the
convention, saying she should not be required to return Shelli to Perú because,
in the words of that provision, “there is a grave risk that his or her return
would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the
child in an intolerable situation.”  She says there is a grave risk of
harassment, psychological abuse and physical abuse at the hands of the father
and his family and a grave risk that Shelli would be put in an intolerable
situation if required to return to Perú.  The father denies there is any such
risk, but says if this court finds there is any risk, the courts and
authorities of Perú can deal adequately with it, and the mother has no valid
reason to keep Shelli away from her home country.

[
4
]

If successful in resisting the return of Shelli
to Perú, the mother has asked this court for an order for custody in her favour,
with only supervised access to the father.

Result

[
5
]

The father's application for an order for return
of Shelli to Perú is dismissed, on the ground that the mother has met the onus
under article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention.  She has established that a
return would expose Shelli to grave risk of physical or psychological harm or
place her in an intolerable situation.

[
6
]

The mother's claim for custody and an access
order may proceed.  Directions may be sought if need be, by motion or at a case
conference. If costs are not agreed, they are to be addressed initially in
writing and if desired an oral hearing may be booked.

Family history

[
7
]

The father is 47 years old.  He was born and
raised in Lima, Perú and has always lived there, though he received some of his
education in the USA.  He holds
a senior position in a family business that imports and sells automotive parts.
The mother is 41 years old and was born and raised in Canada.  She is a specialist in a particular computer software.

[
8
]

The mother was working as a computer consultant
and living in New York City
when the parties met on separate vacations in Jamaica in 1999.  They took a liking to each other and arranged to meet
again in Miami, where the father went regularly for business and where his
family owned a condominium in Miami Beach.  The father speaks Spanish and English fluently.  When they met,
the mother spoke English and French but no Spanish.  They dated for a time and
the mother began coming to Lima
on business trips and spending substantial blocks of time with the father.  He
asked her to marry him in 2003.  They were married in a civil ceremony in Montreal on July 26, 2003 and in a
religious ceremony in Lima on
November 17, 2003.

[
9
]

The father and his family are Jewish.  They go
to synagogue, observe the major holidays and consider their Jewishness
important.  The mother was raised Christian but had many Jewish friends in New York and had an interest in Judaism.
It was important to the father and his family that she convert to Judaism if
she and the father were to marry.  She pursued a course of study with a rabbi
and underwent an Orthodox conversion, which allowed the couple to have a
religious marriage ceremony in the father’s synagogue in Lima.  She continues to live as an Orthodox
Jew.  It turns out she is more observant than the father.

[
10
]

The couple lived in Lima in an apartment owned by the father’s family.  He continued to work
in the family business.  The mother did not work at first after the marriage,
though over time she acquired some proficiency in Spanish and pursued and
landed contracts with former clients and new clients.

[
11
]

The couple wanted to have children as soon as
possible but no pregnancy occurred until the end of 2005, after the couple
attempted and then abandoned efforts at in vitro fertilization.  Shelli, their
only child, was born August 19, 2006 in Lima.

[
12
]

According to the mother, the marriage was
troubled from the start and the father became increasingly abusive to her.  The
father painted a picture of an unhappy marriage as well, denying abuse and
minimizing the trouble until later in the marriage.  They separated on
September 10, 2008 in Lima.
The mother continued living in Lima with Shelli and the father had regular visitation until November,
2009.  At that time the mother moved with Shelli to Cusco, Perú, some 1100 kilometres
away.  Her avowed purpose was to get away from the harassment perpetrated by
the father and his family.

[
13
]

Two months later, under court order, the mother
and Shelli returned to Lima.
In late January, 2010, two physical confrontations occurred, one between the
mother and the father and one between the mother and the father’s mother.
Police were called on both occasions and the scenes were very dramatic.  Shelli
witnessed both.

[
14
]

The couple had begun litigation in Lima in respect of custody and access rights
in September, 2008.  Initially cooperative, the parties’ positions became
adversarial and ultimately hostile.  This will be discussed below in detail.

[
15
]

The mother obtained an order permitting her to
travel to Canada with Shelli
for a family visit from September to November, 2010.  She left Perú with Shelli
on September 8, 2010.  She and Shelli have been residing with her parents in Toronto ever since.  The father has had
only a handful of supervised visits with Shelli in the past year.

[
16
]

Shelli had been attending a Jewish day school in
Lima.  She is now enrolled in a
Jewish day school in Toronto.
She is healthy and is in all respects a normal child.

Case history in Perú

[
17
]

Though the two parties are not lawyers or
experts in the court system of Perú, they told me some things about Peruvian family
law, family courts and legal processes in the course of their evidence.  What
they told me coincided with the evidence I had from Peruvian lawyers.

[
18
]

In Ontario, when we speak of “custody” of a child, we speak of a bundle of
rights (and obligations) in respect of the child, such as physical care and
control, the right to determine residence, the right to decide on matters of
health and education, and so on.  In Perú, there are similar notions.  There is
a term,
tenencia
, which the parties agreed denotes physical care and
control, translated in the documents filed at trial as “custody”.  There is
another term,
patria potestad
, translated in the documents as “parental
authority” or “parental rights and duties” and sometimes as “custody”, which the
parties said denotes the decision making authority over a child and,
apparently, the obligations of a parent toward a child.

[
19
]

I also learned from the parties that each time a
person goes to family court for a new order, a new application is filed, which
in turn receives a new file number and is assigned randomly to a particular
judge of the court.  Though the documents refer to the “Nth Family Court of
Lima”, I was told that Lima has
one Family Court in one building with several numbered branches operating on
different floors with several judges sitting within each branch.  If there is
any coordination between the different judges of the Lima Family Court in
respect of the various claims made in different applications between the same
parties, it was not apparent from the court documents and the parties’ evidence
indicated there was none.

[
20
]

The parties also told me that domestic violence
allegations between spouses are handled by the Family Court.  Further, they
said that a domestic violence claim triggers an automatic psychological
evaluation of the complainant.  A claim for a “protective measure”, which in
Ontario would be called a restraining order, may be begun with a complaint to
the police, and if begun in that way, not only is there an automatic
psychological evaluation of the complainant, but also the claim is passed on for
screening to the Provincial Family Attorney’s office (
Fiscalía Provincial de
Familia
), a part of the national government’s attorney general’s ministry (
Ministerio
Público
).  As with the Family Court Judges, there can be several Provincial
Family Attorneys in a province, designated by number.  It appears the office of
a Provincial Family Attorney can refuse to proceed with a complaint or, if
satisfied there are grounds to do so, can issue a temporary protective measure order
that is effective until confirmed, altered or dismissed by a judge in Family
Court.  The judge receiving such a complaint screens it to see if it is
“admissible”, which appears to be a vetting for jurisdiction, standing, proper
form and apparent merit, and, if it is admitted, the judge sends it on for
hearing.  In order to avoid confusion over the use of “admit”, which has a very
different meaning in our law, I will use the word “accept”, which adequately renders
the sense of the Spanish.

[
21
]

The sequence of court events in Perú took on
considerable significance at the trial before me.  Each party accused the other
of using the justice system there improperly and of obtaining orders to which they
were not entitled.  There was, at least to this observer unacquainted with Peruvian
courts and procedures, a confusing thicket of different cases in different
courts, all going on at once.  The parties tried to help sort it out in oral
testimony, but in the end I found it necessary to go through, page by page, the
extensive documentation they provided to me.  Accordingly I will set out in a
chart in an appendix at the end of this decision the chronology as I know it,
on the basis of the court documents from Perú provided to me in evidence.  This
chart is a chronological compilation of events from the court documents provided
to me by the parties.  It also includes other court events about which the
parties gave oral evidence at trial.  There were in addition steps in the
various court cases recorded in a summary chart prepared by the wife, but for
which the court documents were not provided.  Because the documents were not
provided, I have not included many of them in my chart.  There probably are still
more court events and documents I do not know about.

[
22
]

I was provided with English translations of the
original documents, which were in Spanish.  The translations are of very uneven
quality and often contain inconsistent translations of the same terms in Spanish.
Some of the translations are very hard to follow.  Many have not been edited
for consistency or accuracy and some contain passages that are on their face
incorrect or are just plain incomprehensible.  I have, as I told the parties at
the trial, some ability in Spanish.  I am relying on the translations provided
to me, but there are some instances where I have used my own understanding of a
Spanish document provided to correct a clear mistranslation or to try to make
it correspond with the translation of similar terms in another, similar
document.

Case history in Ontario

[
23
]

On learning the mother intended not to return
Shelli to Perú, the father applied for and obtained a Legal Aid lawyer and
filed an application for Shelli’s return to Perú in the Ontario Court of
Justice on December 6, 2010.  The mother retained her own lawyer and filed her
answer on January 24, 2011, in which she opposed the return of Shelli to Perú
and claimed custody of Shelli.  The court heard the case on the basis of
affidavit evidence from both parties on May 27, 2011.  That same day, the court
dismissed the father’s application and made a consent temporary order for the
father to have access in Toronto under supervision.

[
24
]

The father appealed to this court on June 10,
2011.  On July 14, 2011, this court made a temporary order, on consent of the
parties, for the father’s access to Shelli to take place via Skype three times
each week.

[
25
]

For reasons that were not disclosed to me, on
August 30, 2011 the parties consented to an order allowing the appeal, with no
costs to either party.  That order also provided (again on consent) for:
setting aside the OCJ order of May 27, 2011;  directing a trial of the Hague
application to start on November 7, 2011;  declaring the passage of time since
May 27 would not be a factor in the trial;  continuing the access order of July
14 and providing for other access;  and providing for a stay of the order of
this court made after the trial.

[
26
]

By agreement of the parties, approved by the
court at a trial management conference on November 2, 2011, the pleadings
before me at the trial consisted only of the application and answer that had
been filed in the Ontario Court of Justice.

[
27
]

The trial proceeded with an admission at the
start by the mother that her retention of Shelli in Canada was wrongful, within the meaning of the Hague Convention, because
she had left Perú under the authority of an order that required Shelli to be
returned over a year ago.  By agreement of the parties’ lawyers, because the
onus was now (as a result of the admission) on the mother to establish why she
should not be ordered to return Shelli to Perú, the mother went first at the
trial, even though she was the respondent to the father’s application.

Evidence at trial

[
28
]

Some of the oral testimony at the trial was
given in Spanish, with the aid of an interpreter.  Much of the documentary
evidence was in Spanish, accompanied by English translations.  I told the
parties at the start of the trial that I had some capacity in Spanish, but
would rely on the interpreter or the translated documents rather than my own
understanding.  In the course of the trial there were a few occasions when I
picked up a mistranslation or I suggested a translation, but I believe I
obtained confirmation each time from a witness or party or the interpreter, as
the case may be, that I had it right.

[
29
]

The documentary evidence before me included a
number of documents filed in the courts of Perú, some as pleadings, some as
evidence of the parties or other witnesses, some as expert psychological or
medical reports prepared for use by a court and some as findings and orders of
a court.  I was also given letters prepared by Peruvian lawyers in response to
questions put to them about Peruvian law, procedure and courts.  The parties
agreed they were all to be received as evidence and were to be given such
weight, if any, as I considered appropriate.

[
30
]

The lawyers’ letters were of help in
understanding the Peruvian judicial system and the cases in process there.
Where their opinions or conclusions diverge, I am unable to prefer one over the
other as I have no reliable basis for evaluating their relative strengths.

[
31
]

The medical and psychological reports were also
helpful and I have given them the weight such documents would receive if prepared
in Ontario by qualified
physicians or psychologists.  They were prepared by physicians or psychologists
with no connection to the parties, in public institutions established to assist
in court cases in Perú, and were relied on by provincial family attorneys (who
have authority to make temporary orders subject to confirmation by judges) and by
judges in those cases.  I am aware that the information provided to the
professionals was provided by the mother and in some cases by Shelli, without
input by the father, but the professionals also performed their own
examinations and professional assessments.  The father could have, but did not,
submit other reports or assessments or insist the professionals be
crossexamined.  Those reports will receive substantial weight in my decision.

[
32
]

The findings and orders of the Peruvian courts
and provincial family attorneys ought to receive great weight, especially where
both parties were present or represented when the finding or order was made.
Indeed, where both parties were present or represented, they are entitled to
the status of
res judicata
, as the parties fully participated knowing
that the finding or order was intended to have that effect and to be
enforceable by the judicial authorities of Perú.  However, I do not know what
facts were before the Peruvian courts and what the threshold is for making a
finding of psychological or physical abuse under Peruvian law.  Also, sometimes
there were parallel proceedings going on there in which inconsistent findings
or results were reached.  As a result, I must make my own findings of fact on
the issues before me.

[
33
]

I was also given all the notes of Canadian
embassy personnel from Lima and
Department of Foreign Affairs headquarters in Ottawa about the parties and their child, in the guise of business
records.  In my view these records add very little to my understanding of the
facts and issues, other than the surprising fact that the Canadian embassy in Lima has an armoured car and a bodyguard at
its disposal, both of which were used in transporting the mother and Shelli to
the airport on September 8, 2010.  All the information in the notes came from
the parties and their supporters.  The notes neither add to nor detract from
the parties’ own testimony.  The mother suggested that the involvement of
embassy personnel lent weight to what she said, but I disagree.  All that these
notes can do is negate any suggestion – and the father made none – that the
mother’s complaints about the father and his family were recently concocted.  Rather,
the father said the mother’s complaints were from the start fabricated or
grossly exaggerated.

[
34
]

The mother testified at length, followed by her
sister in law and the nanny who cared for Shelli in the parties’ home and in
the mother’s home after the separation, including much of the two months the
mother and Shelli spent in Cusco.  The mother’s only other witness was her
Peruvian lawyer since late 2008, who has now become her legal representative
there under a general power of attorney as well as a friend.  The lawyer
testified only as a fact witness.

[
35
]

The father also testified at length.  His only
other witness was his mother, whom I will call the grandmother, in order to
avoid confusion of her with the mother.

[
36
]

The major events discussed in the witnesses’
testimony were the climate in the parties’ home generally from the date they
began living together as husband and wife;  some incidents following the
separation;  the bruising of Shelli’s legs around June 1, 2009;  the mother’s
sudden relocation to Cusco in November, 2009;  the mother’s trip to Canada in
January, 2010;  the confrontation at the father’s apartment garage on January
25, 2010;  the confrontation at the club on January 29, 2010;  the
circumstances leading up to the mother’s and Shelli’s departure to Canada in
September, 2010.  The witnesses for each side all had personal knowledge of
most of these events, and the mother had knowledge of all of them.

[
37
]

The mother had a good memory for events and
details.  It was obvious she was severely affected by the events in her
marriage and she continued to be emotional when retelling her story or when
listening to others retell their version of events.  She dissolved in tears
when the CD recording made on January 25, 2010 was played.  Her continuing fear
of the father was palpable.  Her oral testimony was generally consistent,
detailed and convincing.  Her oral testimony was, however, sometimes at
variance with documents she put before Peruvian courts about the reasons why
she wanted to travel with Shelli.  Also, for some reason she took the position
that she did not meet the father until well after they first actually met in Jamaica, and she did not acknowledge living
with the father before marriage though it appeared she actually spent more than
just occasional time with him in Lima and Miami.  These inconsistencies were on relatively minor, face saving
matters, and I do not accede to the father's submission that they make her less
credible on the important events.

[
38
]

The father was also reasonably good at recalling
events, but was much less affected by them than the mother and less forthcoming
in details about their lives together.  He was more controlled and more reticent
in his answers.  I formed the impression that he was less inclined to get into
specifics so that he would not have to deny the mother’s detailed recounting of
multiple incidents and provide his own version of them.  He did make some
general denials but I found them unconvincing in the face of all the incidents
reported by the mother and corroborated by others.  He painted the conflicts in
the marriage as a joint and more or less equal responsibility of the parties,
but the evidence showed the mother was defending against rather than
instigating or perpetuating conflicts.  His acceptance of the mother as a
"good mother" before me was in contrast with the positions he took in
the courts of Perú.

[
39
]

The grandmother clearly was invested in
protecting the reputation of her son and herself.  She minimized the parties’
difficulties.  Her interpretation of a birthday card she sent the mother after
the separation as “loving” said much about her reliability:  the card’s
principal contents were to wonder why the mother had changed so much, or
whether she had been pretending all along, and to ask that God should forgive
her.  This was hardly a loving message.  The mother was right in describing it
as a form of harassment.

[
40
]

The mother’s lawyer, admittedly a friend of the
mother, was measured, clear and consistent in her testimony and I found her to
be a credible witness.  She too demonstrated some agitation in recalling the
events she had witnessed.  The nanny was straightforward and credible as well,
and she tried to be and I think succeeded in being even handed toward the
father.  The mother's sister in law's evidence was of no assistance.

[
41
]

In general, I prefer the evidence of the mother
and her witnesses over that of the father and grandmother.  I acknowledge the
mother did gild the lily or even misrepresent her intentions in some of her
Peruvian court documents but I find her testimony about her life with the
father and the confrontations she had with him and his family was generally
reliable.

[
42
]

There was no expert evidence about Shelli's
development or condition after she left Perú or about the risks a return to Perú
might pose to her.  There was some evidence, both expert and non expert, about
the impact of various events in Perú on her and there was evidence by both the
mother and the nanny about her present condition.

Findings respecting various events

[
43
]

I set out below my findings of fact regarding
the major events and incidents described in the evidence before me.

Atmosphere in the home up to the separation date

[
44
]

The father became a very different person, after
the marriage, from the considerate and helpful man who courted the mother.
Despite being the manager of a prosperous family business (in respect of which
the grandmother admitted that shares were transferred back and forth among
family members at the whim of the father’s father), the father called on the mother
to finance – out of her savings, since she had no income – the parties’ household
expenses, their attempts at assisted reproduction and even their honeymoon.
(The father generously agreed to cover the airfare by using travel points
accumulated from his many business trips.  He told her he was going on the
honeymoon trip, and she could come along, or not.)

[
45
]

Having insisted on an Orthodox Jewish
conversion, which the mother embraced, the father and his family ignored the
dietary laws of
kashrut
, which the mother felt she ought to and wanted
to observe.  The father also ignored her religious sexual sensibilities, which
included abstention from sex two weeks out of four for reasons of Orthodox
religious practice.  He insisted on being satisfied orally (at least) and
threatened and at times made good on the threat to seek satisfaction on the
streets when she was unavailable for sexual purposes.

[
46
]

When she finally became pregnant, the doctor (because
of the location of the embryo) warned her against sex in the first four months
of pregnancy, and the father declared that if she thought he would wait four
months, she was kidding herself.  Shortly after that, he returned from a trip
to Miami with boxes of condoms,
clearly not intended for use with the mother.  Seven months pregnant and about
to celebrate her birthday, she asked him not to go away on a scheduled business
trip, but he refused, saying her birthday was like any other day.  So she
accompanied him to Miami on her
birthday, where he told her to keep on going back to Canada.  The reason she did not was mainly financial – she had health
insurance coverage in Perú, but paying for expenses of pregnancy and birth in Canada without coverage could have cost
$30,000-$40,000.  (It turns out the financial concern was warranted:  Shelli
was born by emergency caesarean section.)

[
47
]

The father (and grandmother) told her she should
treat him as the king of the home.  The grandmother added that she should not
be concerned if he consorted with street women, as he had chosen her (not them)
to be his queen.

[
48
]

The father was eager for the mother to find a
job, but he insisted she must be readily available by phone and email when she
finally secured work, even to the point of saying she should tell her bosses
they should wait while she took a call from him.  He would regularly disparage
her to friends in her presence, and would repeatedly abuse her verbally,
demanding apologies for perceived transgressions, failing which she should pack
up and leave “his home” to return to Canada.  There were frequent discussions
of divorce, regular suggestions she should just pack up and go home to Canada, and not infrequent tussles where he
would try to push her out the door of the apartment.  The nanny and a maid were
present for some of these altercations.  One time the father threatened them,
saying they should not get involved or they would not be able to find a job in
Perú again.

[
49
]

From her birth, Shelli was present for these
incidents.  Shortly after she was born, the couple separated and the father
went to live in his parents’ home.  They reconciled just after Shelli’s first
birthday but, in the mother’s words, they were never really together.  Things
came to a head in early September, 2008.  The marriage was clearly ending.
Just before the separation date, the father warned the mother that he would
always have Shelli with him, Perú was his country, it was “a corrupt country
and you never know what can happen” and she should “watch her back”.  To
emphasize his points, the father would touch the “kangaroo” or waist purse he
regularly wore, in which he often carried a handgun.  When the mother's lawyer told
him of the mother's fear about the gun in his bag, he told her he would never
let his gun go, it was his protection.  In his oral testimony, he explained the
need of the gun as resulting from working late into the evening at the family
business, which was in a rough part of town.  Then why touch the waist purse at
all?  Or why wear the waist purse during the day, away from the business premises?
The answer is clear:  intimidation.

[
50
]

The father’s cousin, who was a convicted drug
trafficker, joined in on the threats one day when the mother was out shopping.
He suddenly accosted her in a butcher shop, telling her she was going to die,
he had met people in jail who would do it and it would only take 20 soles [about
$7.50].  That night the mother locked herself in the bedroom, but the father pounded
on the door, persuaded her to unlock it, dragged her out of the bedroom by the
legs despite Shelli’s crying, and refused to allow her to return to the room.

[
51
]

Shortly after that, the father went on a
business trip to Miami and the
mother fled the apartment, with Shelli, to take up residence in an apartment of
her own.  One morning when arriving with Shelli at her nursery school
(accompanied by two other persons in the car as a precaution), the mother
suddenly found the father’s mother and father banging on the car.  She had
hired a lawyer at this time and asked him what to do.  His advice included that
she hire a bodyguard.  She did.  She also began the litigation detailed in the
chart in the appendix, not knowing that the father had actually gone to the
courts first for orders for custody of Shelli and to prevent Shelli from
leaving the country.

[
52
]

The father would have me believe that the mother
was an equal instigator and combatant in all these situations in the home, but
my evaluation of all the evidence (including the psychological expert report of
September 17, 2008) tells me otherwise.  The home was a place of unhappiness,
oppression and abuse for the mother at the hands of the father for many months,
and Shelli was there to experience it too.  I do not have to find the mother
was an entirely innocent party in all this, in order to find the father was by
far the more responsible party.  I accept that he genuinely loves his daughter,
but that did not stop him from engaging in the behaviour set out above.

Incidents following the separation

[
53
]

Following the separation the father at first had
regular, almost daily, access to Shelli.  The mother went to Mexico in October, 2008 on business,
leaving Shelli in the care of her nanny and a maid – and under the protection
of a bodyguard.  The father held on to Shelli at the end of one of his regular
access visits when the mother was still away.  Peruvian law apparently requires
that a child be left in the care of family members only, when a custodial
parent is away, and the father waited until the mother left and then asserted
his right to assume care of Shelli.  The mother received an urgent message from
her then lawyer to return home and discovered the father had Shelli in his
care.  The father told her he would not return Shelli to her unless she agreed
to sign a conciliation (mediation) agreement.  She signed the agreement on
November 6, 2008.  The terms were:  the mother was to have custody (
tenencia

Applicable legislative provisions

[
85
]

Both Canada and Perú are contracting states to the Hague Convention of 25
October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction.  The entire
convention has been incorporated into Ontario domestic law as a schedule to section 46 of the
Children’s Law
Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12.  The provisions of the convention relevant
to this case are:

Convention on the Civil Aspects of
International Child Abduction

The States signatory to the present
Convention,

Firmly convinced that the interests of
children are of paramount importance in matters relating to their custody,

Desiring to protect children
internationally from the harmful effects of their wrongful removal or retention
and to establish procedures to ensure their prompt return to the State of their
habitual residence, as well as to secure protection for rights of access,

Have resolved to conclude a Convention to
this effect and have agreed upon the following provisions:

Chapter I — Scope of the Convention

Article 1

The objects of the present Convention are:

(a) to secure the prompt return of children wrongfully
removed to or retained in any
Contracting

State
; and

(b) to ensure that rights of custody and of access under
the law of one
Contracting
State
are effectively
respected in the other Contracting States.

*     *     *     *     *

Article 3

The removal or the retention of a child is
to be considered wrongful where:

(a) it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a
person, an institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under the
law of the State in which the child was habitually resident immediately before
the removal or retention; and

(b) at the time of removal or retention those rights were
actually exercised, either jointly or alone, or would have been so exercised
but for the removal or retention.

The rights of custody mentioned in
sub-paragraph (a) above, may arise in particular by operation of law or by
reason of a judicial or administrative decision, or by reason of an agreement
having legal effect under the law of that State.

*     *     *     *     *

Article 5

For the purposes of this Convention:

(a) ‘rights of custody’ shall include rights relating to
the care of the person of the child and, in particular, the right to determine
the child’s place of residence;

(b) ‘rights of access’ shall include the right to take a
child for a limited period of time to a place other than the child’s habitual
residence.

*     *     *     *     *

Chapter III --- Return of Children

*     *     *     *     *

Article 12

Where a child has been wrongfully removed
or retained in terms of Article 3 and, at the date of commencement of the
proceedings before the judicial or administrative authority of the Contracting
State where the child is, a period of less than one year has elapsed from the
date of the wrongful removal or retention, the authority concerned shall order
the return of the child forthwith.

*     *     *     *     *

Article 13

Despite the provisions of the preceding
Article, the judicial or administrative authority of the requested State is not
bound to order the return of the child if the person, institution or other body
which opposes its return establishes that:

(a) the person, institution or other body having the care
of the person of the child was not actually exercising the custody rights at
the time of removal or retention, or had consented to or subsequently
acquiesced in the removal or retention; or

(b) there is a grave risk that his or her return would
expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child
in an intolerable situation.

*     *     *     *     *

Article 14

In ascertaining whether there has been a
wrongful removal or retention within the meaning of Article 3, the judicial or
administrative authorities of the requested State may take notice directly of
the law of, and of judicial or administrative decisions, formally recognized or
not in the State of the habitual residence of the child, without recourse to
the specific procedures for the proof of that law or for the recognition of
foreign decisions which would otherwise be applicable.

*     *     *     *     *

Article 16

After receiving notice of a wrongful
removal or retention of a child in the sense of Article 3, the judicial or
administrative authorities of the Contracting State to which the child has been
removed or in which it has been retained shall not decide on the merits of
rights of custody until it has been determined that the child is not to be
returned under this Convention or unless an application under this Convention
is not lodged within a reasonable time following receipt of the notice.

[
86
]

The mother in this case has conceded that both
the father and the courts of Perú were exercising rights of custody within the

November 8, 2010 was a wrongful retention, that article 12 is applicable and that

ordering Shelli's return to Perú as mandated by article 12.

[
87
]

The father's lawyer submitted that article 13
(b) should be interpreted so that the phrase "there is a grave risk that
his or return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm …"
referred to the return of the parent (in this case, the mother) as exposing the

"opposing
its
return" (my emphasis) when talking about
the return of the child, whereas (b) uses "his or her" rather than
"its" and so must be taken to be referring to someone other than the

Chapter III, of which article 13 is part, is headed "Return of
Children".  The heading helps clarify whose return is at issue.  Fortunately

her" in the English version is referring to the child.  The French version
(with emphasis added) is:

b) qu’il
existe un risque grave que
le retour de l’enfant
ne l’expose à un
danger physique ou psychique, ou de toute autre manière ne le place dans une
situation intolérable.

Cases interpreting article 13 (b)

[
90
]

The highest authority in Canada on article 13 (b) is the Supreme
Court's decision in
Thomson v. Thomson
,
1994 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 551.  In that
case, the parties married and separated in Scotland.  The Scottish court had made a temporary custody order in favour
of the mother and a non removal order.  The mother left Scotland with the child nevertheless, to
visit her parents in Manitoba, and
applied for custody there.  The Scottish court then granted final custody to
the father in what has become known as a "chasing order".  The
mother's departure in the face of the Scottish order was ruled wrongful and she
was ordered to return the child to Scotland, but only on the basis of
undertakings given by the father to restore the status quo, including having the
child remain in the mother's care.  The court commented on the "grave
risk" test in article 13 (b) of the convention as follows:

80
It has been
generally accepted that the Convention mandates a more stringent test than that
advanced by the appellant.  In brief, although the word "grave"
modifies "risk" and not "harm", this must be read in conjunction
with the clause "
or otherwise

place
the child in an intolerable situation".  The use of the word
"otherwise" points inescapably to the conclusion that the physical or
psychological harm contemplated by the first clause of Article 13(b) is harm to
a degree that also amounts to an intolerable situation.  Examples of cases
that have come to this conclusion are:

Gsponer
v. Johnstone

(1988), 12 Fam. L.R. 755 (Fam. Ct. Aust. (Full
Ct.));

Re A. (A Minor)
(Abduction)
,

[1988] 1 F.L.R. 365 (Eng. C.A.);

Re A. and another (Minors)
(Abduction:  Acquiescence)
,

[1992] 1 All E.R. 929 (C.A.)
;

Re L. (Child Abduction)
(Psychological Harm)
,

[1993] 2 F.L.R. 401 (Eng. H.C. (Fam. Div.));

appointed to deal with Hague Convention cases to discuss how to proceed and to
explore the possibilities under option 2 or option 3 below that would be
enforceable in Perú.

2.  Consider and adopt appropriate undertakings to be required of
the father before ordering the child to be returned to Perú, so as to eliminate
or alleviate risks of harm to the child or of an intolerable situation for the
child.

3.  Consider and adopt appropriate temporary orders designed to
eliminate or alleviate risks of harm to the child or of an intolerable
situation for the child.

4.  Decline to order the child's return because undertakings or
temporary orders can not be expected to eliminate or alleviate risks of harm to
the child or of an intolerable situation for the child.

[
121
]

The father's lawyer invited me to pursue option
1, with the parties' lawyers taking part.  He referred me to
Hoole v. Hoole
,

2008 BCSC 1248
, a decision of Martinson J., British Columbia's liaison judge,
in which she outlined the procedure she followed in a case where there was a
parallel case going on in Oregon.  The case dealt with some of the concerns or
problems involved in having direct contact between judges of two
jurisdictions.  Some of the potential problems (not present in
Hoole
) included
the use of different languages and different legal concepts or terminology as
impediments to effective communication or cooperation.  I have experienced both
of these problems in the case before me.  In
Hoole
it was suggested that
those problems should not usually be serious impediments.

[
122
]

I wish I could share the optimism of Martinson
J., but my experience with the translation and interpretation in this case as
well as my general experience over the last 16 years in Ontario courts tells me
that language and terminology issues can pose significant problems and the translation
and interpretation resources to deal with them are often lacking.  See
Eliassen
,
above, where communication between British and Norwegian judges was in some
respects unsatisfactory and was not followed up.  Nonetheless I would certainly
consider such direct communication in an appropriate case, even if the other
jurisdiction involved used a different language from our official languages and
had a different legal system.  However, as will be seen below in my
consideration of the other three options, I have concluded that the assistance
of the Peruvian liaison judge would not provide an answer to the real problems
in this case.

[
123
]

Options 2 and 3 have been mandated for
consideration by courts hearing Hague Convention cases in which the article 13
(b) threshold has been met.  See
Thomson
, extracts quoted at pars. [90]-[91]
of this decision, and the cases cited at par. [99] of this decision.  However,
I think this is one of those cases where undertakings by the father or
transitory or temporary orders by this court will not have the desired effect.
First, an undertaking or order could bind only the father -- but the father's
other family members have been significant actors in creating the harm or the
intolerable situation and, not being parties to this case, would not be bound.
Second, undertakings, even if collected from the father and all of his family
members, would not prevent the Peruvian authorities, and in particular the
prosecutors or the judiciary involved in criminal and defamation cases pending against
the mother or in civil court order enforcement remedies against the mother,
from pursuing arrest or imprisonment of the mother.  Third, an undertaking to
this court or an order of this court, if disobeyed, could not give rise to
effective enforcement by contempt over a person out of this jurisdiction.
Finally and most importantly, I am convinced from the history of this case that
the father and his family members have not felt themselves bound to follow
court orders in the past and would not hesitate to disobey them in the future.
The same would be true of undertakings given to this court or the courts of
Perú.

[
124
]

For these reasons I find the appropriate remedy
in this case is option 4, dismissal of the father's application for an order
requiring the return of Shelli to Perú.

Forum shopping or abuse of process

[
125
]

The father asserted there was no reported case
like this one, in which the mother actively litigated the custody, access,
support and domestic violence issues in the courts of Perú both before and
after returning to Canada and participating
in litigation here.  She even has appeals pending at the Supreme Court of Perú
against decisions rendered before her departure from the country.  The father
submitted that she had attorned to the jurisdiction of Perú and should not be
permitted to invoke the aid of the courts of a second jurisdiction, Ontario.

[
126
]

This is not a case of attornment.  Until
November, 2010, the mother was doing exactly as she should have done:  she was
pursuing legal remedies in Perú, where she, the father and Shelli all still resided.
There was nowhere else for her to pursue such legal recourse.  From November,
2010 onward, she continued to participate in pending cases but launched no new
ones of her own, other than appeals in pending cases, with one possible
exception:  she asked for an extension to the two month travel authorization
she had obtained, trying to obtain permission for an extended stay here.  (I
say possible because it is not clear, from the materials I have, just when she
asked for the extension -- it could have been in September or October.)  She
did not and still does not know, until the appeal period from this decision
expires or an appeal from this decision is decided, whether she is going to
have to go back to Perú.  It would have been risky and even foolish for her not
to continue to defend her rights there.

[
127
]

The mother did not institute this application in
Ontario -- the father did.  Served
with a Hague Convention application for an order to return Shelli to Perú, the
mother of course defended and added a custody claim, which can proceed only if
she is able to keep Shelli here.  On December 9, 2010, when the Lima Family
Court made a chasing order giving the father temporary custody of Shelli, the
mother was deprived of the ability to ask the Ontario Courts to recognize and
enforce her custody rights extending back to the conciliation agreement of
November 6, 2008.  She had no realistic alternative but to make a fresh custody
claim.  It will be open to the father, if the claim proceeds, to assert any
defences he may have to that claim.

[
128
]

I fail to see how the mother has committed an
abuse of process.

[
129
]

On the issue of forum shopping, the father had the Hague Convention application as his first
remedy, subject to a successful article 13 (b) defence.  Now that the article
13 (b) defence has succeeded, he still has his defences to the mother's claim
for custody under the
Children's Law Reform Act
, including a submission that
Ontario should or must decline
jurisdiction on the grounds provided in the statute, though he will be bound by
the findings of fact in this decision.

Custody and access

[
130
]

The mother's custody claim is now entitled to
proceed.  I leave it to counsel to decide whether a fresh application by the
mother should replace the claim asserted in her answer filed a year or so ago.
If the parties are unable to agree on how to proceed, they should book a motion
for directions to come before me, if available.  They may, if desired, address
both the merits of and the procedure for the case at a case conference rather
than move for directions.

Costs

[
131
]

If costs are not settled by agreement, they will
need to be addressed initially in writing.  The mother must serve a written
argument of not more than five pages (plus costs summary, offers and
authorities).  The father may serve a similar response.  The mother may serve a
three page reply (plus authorities).  Either party may book a one hour costs
hearing with me.  The mother is responsible for getting the costs submissions
to me.
